catalog_quote: 2.9 Stress. Word stress is predictable in CDA, and follows a number of rules that are common amongst other conservative Arabic dialects, as in MSA. 43 These can be summarised as follows in descending order. a. The final superheavy syllables CvCC and Cv̄ C are stressed if present, e.g., māṣūr 'guts', halūmāt 'dreams', and ġallēt 'fog, mist'. b. If superheavy syllables are absent, stress the rightmost non-final heavy syllable Cv̄ or CvC. In trisyllabic or greater forms, stress lands on the ante-penultimate syllable, e.g., xātim 'ring', mubannad 'closed', and murtafaʕ 'high'. c. In all other circumstances, stress falls on the leftmost light syllable Cv, e.g., wārā 'behind', waraqa 'paper', and šarika 'a company'. d. Basic verb stems demonstrate iambic stress patterns, with stress falling on the second heavy syllable CvC, e.g., ktub 'he wrote', fṭan 'he remembered', and waṣal 'he arrived'. …

audit.reasoning: The 'weight' coding rests on the only modern descriptive grammar of the language (Davey 2013 thesis = Davey 2016 Brill), held as an open-access PDF, with the deciding §2.9 passage confirmed verbatim on p. 68: final superheavy CvCC/Cv̄C stressed, else rightmost non-final heavy Cv̄/CvC, else leftmost light; verb stems iambic. The century-older Rhodokanakis 1911 grammar, also held, independently states that long vowels and geminates hold the stress against a rightward drift, consistent with weight sensitivity. No later phonology/prosody study of Dhofari Arabic was found in OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar; Glottolog lists no other descriptive work. Only improvement would be checking the paywalled Brill chapter for rewording; nothing suggests the classification would change. Minor locator nit: section is on p. 68, not 68-69.

tone.quote: § 1. Der Akzent.¹ a) Die im ʿOmânî schon konstatierte Tendenz des Druckes, möglichst dem Wortende zuzustreben (Reinhardt, § 95 g. E.), ist im Ḏfârî noch durchgreifender als in jenem und in den Dialekten des Ḥaḍrami und Datînî. ... c) Weil die Schallverstärkung einer Silbe im Druck durch die größere oder geringere Annäherung der Stimmbänder bewirkt wird, ... ¹ „Ton“, „Druck“, „Akzent“ werden im folgenden ohne Bedeutungsunterschied gebraucht.
tone.locator: p. 67, Grammatik A. Lautlehre § 1 a, c and footnote 1
tone.translation: § 1. The accent. a) The tendency of the stress, already noted for ʿOmânî, to move as far as possible toward the end of the word is even more thoroughgoing in Ḏfârî than there and in the dialects of Ḥaḍrami and Datînî. ... c) Since the reinforcement of a syllable under stress is produced by greater or lesser approximation of the vocal cords, ... Fn. 1: 'Ton', 'Druck', 'Akzent' are used below without difference of meaning.
tone.summary: Accent treated purely as dynamic stress; 'Ton' is explicitly a synonym of stress. Pitch appears only for sung/recited verse melody; no statement on lexical tone or its absence.
